verdict: Caution: lend to downstream service and fabrication SMEs tied to the BPCL Kochi refinery programme, not to refiners or traders; structure tightly and take monthly GRM and throughput data.
title: Kochi Petroleum Refining & Coal Products: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
Refining buys crude, runs it through a plant, and sells products; cash is made on the spread between crude cost and product price, not on volume alone. **The whole credit story sits in that spread and in working capital, not in the plant.** Crude is bought at landed cost and product is sold at a posted price, so inventory value swings with Brent; BPCL's Q2 call notes Brent around $70 per barrel from mid-July [4]. So when a proposal lands, check the crude price assumption in the projections; if it is a single flat number, ask for a sensitivity at a higher and lower Brent.

## Where value and cash sit
**Value sits in the refining margin; cash sits in inventory and receivables.** HPCL's 2QFY27 shows GRM at US$32.2/bbl, up 35% QoQ and 262% YoY, on throughput of 6.2mmt, down 5% QoQ and 6% YoY [7] — margin-led, not volume-led. IOC's domestic under-recovery was INR 184 per cylinder in September and INR 229 in October, projected at INR 309 in November and INR 370 in December [6]. So when a proposal lands, check whether the borrower's margin depends on a subsidy or under-recovery that is already rising; if it does, ask how the gap is funded and by when.

## What has changed now
**National output is shrinking while Kerala's tax base is growing.** IIP for NIC 19 is -0.6% YoY and -0.9% Apr-to-date [D], yet Kerala GST collections are +10.3% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1% [D]. Exports are +37.1% Apr-to-date in USD [D]. The local sources on the BPCL Kochi refinery expansion are only headline pages with no figures [1][2][3], so treat the expansion as a pipeline, not a number. **We have no city-level output or margin data for Kochi; collect from customer.**

## Where to grow, and how to grow safely
**Pursue fabrication, mechanical and electrical contracting, catalyst and chemical supply, tank and pipeline maintenance, and logistics SMEs serving the refinery programme.** Avoid standalone crude traders, single-client coal-product units, and any borrower whose receivable is one PSU bill with no fallback. Take monthly GRM and throughput from the refiner's disclosures, monthly GST returns, and quarterly stock statements; covenant a minimum DSCR and a receivables cap. **Rating reports on HPCL, HMEL and CPCL show stable outlooks and regulatory compliance, but CPCL's net-zero target of 2046 is a distant risk, not a current one [8][9].**

## Early-warning signs
- **Monthly (GST and bank statements):** falling turnover or rising receivable days -> freeze limit enhancement and ask for the refiner's payment schedule.
- **Monthly (refiner disclosures):** GRM falling sharply from the US$32.2/bbl level [7] -> reprice the facility and cut tenor.
- **Quarterly (under-recovery):** the IOC gap widening past INR 370 per cylinder [6] -> ask how the borrower is funding the shortfall.
- **Quarterly (IIP NIC 19):** output staying negative [D] -> shift new sanctions to service contracts, not product trading.
